subject: MGMT464
title: Hurdle 1 · The Burning Village — Who Is a Leader, and What Skills Do Leaders Need?

questions.stem: Describe the textbook's central claim in the Amazon opening case.
options: Leadership is often the deciding factor in whether an organisation succeeds or fails, and leadership skills can be developed
Success is decided by market luck
questions.why: Leadership is the difference, and it can be learned. See §1.1.

questions.stem: Identify the leadership choice behind Amazon's early years.
options: Accepting low profits for years to build scale — a long-term, customer-obsessed strategy
Maximising profit in the first year
questions.why: Direction was a leadership choice, not a market accident. See §1.1.

questions.stem: Explain why the 'Day 1' mentality counts as leadership.
options: The leader wrote the culture and enforced it through hiring, meetings and rewards
The staff invented it on their own
questions.why: Leaders shape the culture. See §1.1.

questions.stem: Identify the UAE parallel the chapter gives for leadership making the difference.
options: Emirates airline — from two leased aircraft in 1985 to a global carrier under long-serving leadership
questions.why: Same test: would the outcome have been the same with different leaders? See §1.1.

questions.stem: Describe the textbook definition of leadership.
options: The influencing process of leaders and followers to achieve organisational objectives through change
Giving orders from a formal position
questions.why: Every word carries one of the five key elements. See §1.2.

questions.stem: Identify the five key elements of leadership.
options: Leaders–followers, influence, organisational objectives, change, people
questions.why: Five key elements in one definition. See §1.2.

questions.stem: Explain why influence 'runs both ways' between leaders and followers.
options: Good followers influence leaders, and good leaders were good followers — the question is who is influencing whom right now
questions.why: Leaders–followers element. See §1.2.

questions.stem: Differentiate leadership from the exercise of power.
options: Leaders influence followers toward shared objectives; a leader who serves only himself is exercising power, not leadership
questions.why: Organisational objectives, not personal ones. See §1.2.

questions.stem: Describe the textbook's view on leaders and managers.
options: A manager holds a formal position; a leader may or may not — managers should be leaders, and leaders may be found anywhere
questions.why: Managerial leadership means both together. See §1.3.

questions.stem: Identify the manager's source of influence in the comparison table.
questions.why: Managers: formal position; leaders: relationships, expertise, character. See §1.3.

questions.stem: Differentiate the focus of a manager from the focus of a leader.
options: Manager: planning, organising, controlling — doing things right; leader: direction, alignment, motivation — doing the right things
questions.why: Doing things right vs doing the right things. See §1.3.

questions.stem: Explain why the course is called Leadership AND Management.
options: The distinction is useful but the separation is false — organisations need managers who lead
questions.why: Managers who lead. See §1.3.

questions.stem: Identify the three managerial leadership skills.
questions.why: Three skills; the mix changes with level. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Describe where technical skills matter most.
options: First-line supervisors, who must know the work they oversee
questions.why: Highest at the first line. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Identify the skill that matters equally at every level.
questions.why: The skill that never stops mattering. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Explain why decision-making skill matters most at the top.
options: Problems at the top are least structured, so conceptualising situations and selecting alternatives matters most
Top leaders do the technical work
It is easier at the top
questions.why: Most important at the top. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Identify Mintzberg's three categories of managerial roles.
questions.why: Ten roles in three categories. See §1.5.

questions.stem: Identify the three interpersonal roles.
questions.why: Interpersonal: figurehead, leader, liaison. See §1.5.

questions.stem: Describe the disturbance handler role.
options: Gathering information by reading and observing
questions.why: A decisional role. See §1.5.

questions.stem: Explain why a CEO and a café supervisor play the same ten roles.
options: The roles are universal; only the scale differs — the CEO negotiates aircraft orders, the supervisor negotiates a shift swap
questions.why: That is why leadership can be practised at any level. See §1.5.

questions.stem: Identify the three levels of leadership analysis.
questions.why: The textbook is organised around them. See §1.6.

questions.stem: Describe the individual level of analysis.
options: The dyadic process — the leader and one follower: traits, behaviour, motivation, influence
The leader and the whole organisation
questions.why: Individual = dyadic. See §1.6.

questions.stem: Identify the topics studied at the organisational level.
options: Transformational leadership, culture, ethics, diversity, strategy and change
questions.why: The leader and the organisation as a system. See §1.6.

questions.stem: Explain why the three levels matter for the project interview.
options: A leader strong at one level and weak at another is the most common — and most interesting — finding
Only one level is ever relevant
The interview asks only about traits
questions.why: Ask at all three levels. See §1.6.

questions.stem: Identify the four leadership theory paradigms in order.
questions.why: Each answered a question the last could not. See §1.7.

questions.stem: Describe the question the behavioural paradigm asked.
options: What personal characteristics make a leader?
Which style works in which situation?
How do trait, behaviour and situation combine?
questions.why: Behavioural (1950s →). See §1.7.

questions.stem: Explain the chapter's answer to 'born or made'.
options: Mostly made — traits help, but behaviour and fit to the situation decide
questions.why: Bezos is explained better by what he did and when. See §1.7.

questions.stem: Differentiate a leadership theory from a paradigm.
options: A theory explains some aspect of leadership; a paradigm is a shared mindset — a fundamental way of thinking about leadership
A paradigm is a smaller theory
questions.why: Theory vs paradigm. See §1.7.

questions.stem: Describe the management paradigm the textbook calls 'old'.
options: Stability and control, competition between units, uniformity, the manager as hero who decides alone
questions.why: The leader in charge, stable, controlling. See §1.8.

questions.stem: Identify a feature of the leadership paradigm.
options: Higher purpose — the follower's success is the leader's success
questions.why: Collaboration, diversity, humility. See §1.8.

questions.stem: Explain why the shift to the leadership paradigm happened.
options: Faster change, better-educated employees, flatter organisations, global competition — and AI, which removes the manager's control of information as a source of authority
questions.why: When information is everywhere, influence must come from somewhere else. See §1.8.

questions.stem: Explain the chapter's answer to 'Can a company be led without a leader?'.
options: Systems can run a stable business for a while; they cannot make it change — that is when the absence of leadership shows
No, not even for a day
questions.why: Systems cannot make change happen. See §1.8.

questions.stem: Analyse the burning village: nobody is in charge and people run in circles. Determine what Captain Rami must supply first, in the textbook's terms.
options: Direction — leaders create the direction; the outcome would differ with a different leader
questions.why: Leaders create the direction. See §1.1.

questions.stem: Analyse Rami's decision to take the long mountain road rather than the quick valley path the gang expects. Classify it using the chapter's Amazon parallel.
options: A hard call — a leadership bet many would refuse, like AWS and Kindle
questions.why: Leaders make the hard calls. See §1.1.

questions.stem: Determine the evidence that would show Rami's leadership, not luck, saved the village.
options: The outcome would not have been the same with a different leader
questions.why: The textbook's testable claim. See §1.1.

questions.stem: Classify Noor's act when she convinces Rami to change the plan before he gives any order.
options: Followers influencing the leader — influence runs both ways
questions.why: Good followers influence leaders. See §1.2.

questions.stem: Analyse a village elder who makes everyone work only to protect his own house. Determine which key element is missing.
options: Organisational objectives — he serves himself, so it is power, not leadership
questions.why: Shared goals, not personal ones. See §1.2.

questions.stem: Determine the element Rami uses when he explains the rescue plan, wins the villagers' acceptance and motivates them to carry it out.
options: Influence — communicating ideas, gaining acceptance and motivating support
questions.why: Without influence there is no leadership. See §1.2.

questions.stem: Analyse Omar, who follows Rami only because the captain can punish him. Determine the chapter's verdict.
options: He is being managed, not led — results in the short run, but no change or commitment
He is a follower who influences
questions.why: Following because you must vs because you are influenced. See §1.2.

questions.stem: Classify Rami's position: he holds no title in the village, yet people follow his plan. Determine what this shows.
options: A leader may be found without a formal position — influence comes from relationships, expertise and character
questions.why: Leaders may be found anywhere. See §1.3.

questions.stem: Analyse the village mayor, who writes schedules and checks supplies but gives no direction. Determine the chapter's description.
options: A manager who is not leading — doing things right, not the right things
questions.why: Planning, organising, controlling. See §1.3.

questions.stem: Select the ideal the chapter describes for Rami once the village elects him chief.
options: A manager who leads — uses the position to influence, not only to instruct
questions.why: The ideal: a manager who leads and a leader who can manage. See §1.3.

questions.stem: Analyse Omar, who can climb any wall but cannot persuade a frightened villager. Determine the skill he lacks.
questions.why: Interpersonal: understanding and working with people. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Determine the skill Rami uses most when he must choose between three unclear routes with no map.
options: Decision-making skills — conceptualising the situation and selecting alternatives
questions.why: Most important where problems are least structured. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Classify the head barista in the chapter's table by skill mix.
options: High technical, high interpersonal, lower decision-making
questions.why: First-line: technical and interpersonal high. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a new site engineer promoted to director-general. Determine how her skill mix should change.
options: Technical becomes less important, decision-making more; interpersonal stays high
questions.why: The proportion changes as you rise. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Classify Rami standing in front of the village to receive the elders' blessing before the journey.
questions.why: Represents the unit at ceremonies. See §1.5.

questions.stem: Classify Dana riding ahead to question travellers about the gang's movements.
questions.why: Gathers information: reads, listens, observes. See §1.5.

questions.stem: Classify Rami deciding that the last rope goes to Omar rather than Noor.
questions.why: Decides who gets what, when. See §1.5.

questions.stem: Classify the branch manager in Exercise 1 who decides which two of five staff get the training places.
questions.why: Exercise 1, case C. See §1.5.

questions.stem: Classify the project lead who calls a supplier to settle a dispute before it reaches the client.
questions.why: Exercise 1, case E. See §1.5.

questions.stem: Classify Rami's one-to-one talk that calms Noor's fear on the first night.
questions.why: The leader and one follower. See §1.6.

questions.stem: Classify Rami's work of setting the rules, roles and meetings for his team of three.
questions.why: The leader and the team. See §1.6.

questions.stem: Analyse an interview with a leader who is brilliant with individuals but whose organisation has no strategy. Determine the chapter's reading.
options: Strong at one level and weak at another — the most common and most interesting finding
questions.why: Ask at all three levels. See §1.6.

questions.stem: Classify a villager who says Rami leads because 'he was simply born brave'.
options: Trait paradigm thinking — and the evidence says mostly made
questions.why: Born or made is the trait question. See §1.7.

questions.stem: Classify the question 'Should Rami give orders in the storm but ask opinions at camp?'.
options: Contingency paradigm — which style works in which situation
questions.why: It depends on leader, followers and situation. See §1.7.

questions.stem: Classify an explanation of why Rami's followers commit and change that combines his traits, his behaviour and the situation.
questions.why: Charismatic, transformational, servant theories. See §1.7.

questions.stem: Analyse Rami, who shares information openly, asks the three followers for ideas and lets Dana lead the river crossing. Classify the paradigm.
options: Leadership paradigm — collaboration, shared influence, developing others
Management paradigm — the hero decides alone
questions.why: Humble leader listens, involves, develops others. See §1.8.

questions.stem: Analyse the Crow gang chief, who hides all information and decides everything himself. Classify the paradigm.
options: Management paradigm — control, the hero decides alone
questions.why: Stability, control, the manager as hero. See §1.8.

questions.stem: Select the two Exercise 1 cases that most clearly show the leadership paradigm.
options: B — the café owner teaching a new barista — and F — the team leader proposing a new booking system
questions.why: Developing others and initiating change. See §1.8.

questions.stem: Analyse a village that ran well on rules for years but cannot respond when the gang attacks. Determine what the chapter says this reveals.
options: The absence of leadership — systems cannot make the organisation change
questions.why: Answer to question 4. See §1.8.

questions.stem: Determine the key element shown when Rami convinces the village to abandon its old plan and try a new route.
options: Change — leaders exist to make change happen
questions.why: Influencing and setting objectives is about change. See §1.2.

questions.stem: Classify Rami bargaining with a boatman for passage across the river in return for guarding his cargo.
questions.why: Bargains for the unit with others. See §1.5.

questions.stem: Analyse the chapter's view on followership. Determine why the course also teaches followers.
options: Followership is part of leadership — an effective follower influences the leader, and most leaders also follow someone
questions.why: Followers matter too. See §1.3.

questions.stem: Determine which skill the degree builds and which two this course builds, as the chapter puts it.
options: The degree builds technical skill; the course builds interpersonal and decision-making skill — the ones that get you promoted
questions.why: For you. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Analyse the village elder who says 'the village was saved by good weather'. Determine the textbook's reply.
options: Leadership is often the deciding factor — the test is whether the outcome would have been the same with a different leader
questions.why: The textbook's claim is testable. See §1.1.

questions.stem: Rami spends the night planning how the whole valley's villages will defend themselves together. Classify the level of analysis.
options: Organisational level — the leader and the system as a whole
questions.why: Strategy and change belong to the organisational level. See §1.6.

questions.stem: Noor asks 'what does Rami actually DO that makes people follow?'. Classify the paradigm behind her question.
options: Behavioural paradigm — what effective leaders do
questions.why: What do effective leaders DO? See §1.7.
